What is a phase table?

Phase tables contain rows of transmit phases that are used for each pulse in a pulse sequence. Each row contains one receiver phase item as well.

How is a phase table used?

A phase table can be used in two ways:

  1. accumulates=false A row in the table is applied to all transients in a 1D acquisition. In the next 1D acquisition, the phases in the next row in the table is used. When there are no more rows in the table, the first row is used again. In other words, acquire() uses one row at a time.

  2. accumulates=true The number of transients in a 1D acquisition will be adjusted to be a multiple of the number of rows in the phase table. For the first transient, the phases from the first row are used. For the next transient, the next row is used. If there are more transients and no more rows to use, it starts back at the first row again.

What about simultaneous pulses on multiple channels?

In a pulse sequence, there can be either (or both) single pulses and simultaneous pulses. Single pulses have one column in a phase table entry. Simultaneous pulses have two columns in a phase table.

For example, consider a pulse sequence: Single pulse (1), simultaneous pulse (2), single pulse (3).

Adding a phase table entry like this would:

  • Set the transmit phase for pulse 1 to 0
  • Set the transmit phase for pulse 2 to 90 on the primary channel and 180 on the secondary channel
  • Set the transmit phase for pulse 3 to 270
  • Set the receiver phase to 90
phaseTable.addEntry({0, 90, 180, 270}, 90)

See cosy.lua for a more complete example.

Debugging phase tables

It is possible to get a description of the pulse phases (and other pulse information) that is used for the first transient in a 1D acquisition.

If you have a pulse sequence object named pulseSequence, you can log the information like this:

log(pulseSequence:toString())

If your experiment takes a long time to complete and you would first like to verify the pulse sequences used, you can add this after the configuration section of your experiment:

setNoAcquire(true)

When you have verified your pulse sequences are correct, then you can remove that statement (or set it to false) and re-run your experiment.

Using a different scale for the phases

The default scale for the phases is 0 to 360. If you would like to use a different number to represent the 360 state, use PhaseTable:setStates360()

For example, if you want to use the number 4 as the top end of the scale, you can do this:

pt = PhaseTable()
pt:setStates360(4)
pt:addEntries {
   {0, 1, 2, 3, 0}
}
core:usePhaseTable(pt)
